acts.headline: the non-simulator part of one training episode costs 46 s on the released code. Over 22,000 episodes that is 282 h (11.8 days) on a V100, before any simulator time.
headline_items: the non-simulator part of one training episode costs 46 s on the released code. Over 22,000 episodes that is 282 h (11.8 days) on a V100, before any simulator time.
Where it goes: 56% is one Python loop in ground-projection (label_pooling), 30% is per-ray Python loops in the NeRF feature code. The GPU is only ~9% busy.
Two small patches give numerically identical outputs and run 2.81x faster (46 s -> 16.4 s/episode; 22,000 episodes -> 100 h). The first patch alone gives 2.24x.

acts.headline: at the reporter's setting (batch 2, 64^3) the script costs 6.60 s/step on a V100. The appendix schedule (444,150 steps) = 34 days on V100, 16.5 days on the reporter's A100 (their 3.2 s/step).
headline_items: at the reporter's setting (batch 2, 64^3) the script costs 6.60 s/step on a V100. The appendix schedule (444,150 steps) = 34 days on V100, 16.5 days on the reporter's A100 (their 3.2 s/step).
Where it goes: 54% backward, 22% encode/decode, 25% pure housekeeping (gc.collect every step plus empty_cache about 250 times per step). The data pipeline proxy is not the bottleneck.
Skipping gc/empty_cache gives 4.57 s/step (-31%); adding fp16 autocast gives 2.32 s/step (2.85x total, 11.9 days; numerics not validated).

acts.headline: batch 4 at 500,040 bases measured 3.75 s/step and 9.75 GiB TensorFlow peak (16.4 GiB observed by nvidia-smi); the reported `cudaSetDevice` failure is consistent with overlapping TensorFlow workers reserving the same GPU.
headline_items: batch 4 at 500,040 bases measured 3.75 s/step and 9.75 GiB TensorFlow peak (16.4 GiB observed by nvidia-smi); the reported `cudaSetDevice` failure is consistent with overlapping TensorFlow workers reserving the same GPU.

The issue log says `Auto-computed batch_size=8` and `seq_len=500040` despite outer `--batch_size 4 --seq_len 4000000`; current Paludamentum exposes nested `tiberius.batch_size`, `tiberius.seq_len`, and `tiberius.max_parallel` (default unlimited; set `max_parallel: 1` on a single GPU).
Batch 1/2/4 growth runs: 2.04/3.41/3.75 s median per 500,040-base batch; TensorFlow peaks 2.50/4.98/9.75 GiB. Batch 8 completed at a 24,000 MB cap in 4.39 s with 18.98 GiB TensorFlow peak.

acts.headline: the released script costs 3.9 s per step (batch 2) on a V100 = about 8.1 h per epoch (12,000 train + 3,000 val images) vs the M1's 18-24 h. A V100 is only 2.2-3x faster, not 50-100x.
headline_items: the released script costs 3.9 s per step (batch 2) on a V100 = about 8.1 h per epoch (12,000 train + 3,000 val images) vs the M1's 18-24 h. A V100 is only 2.2-3x faster, not 50-100x.
Why: the loader is single-process (num_workers=0, hard-coded for M1) and spends 0.8-1.1 s of CPU per 1,700x2,200 image; the GPU step is only 0.18-0.48 s.

Fixes measured: 4 workers = 0.47 s/step (8x), 8 workers + fp16 = 0.24 s/step; fp16 instead of the hard-coded bf16 (emulated on Volta) = 2.7x on the GPU part; batch 16 = 3x less per image. 10 epochs: 81 h released vs about 5-10 h fixed.

acts.headline: Paper SOD 0.6B is 120 steps at 1,052.3 s/step; issue reports 1,042 s/step, only 1% apart. The released script defaults to about 469 steps, explaining roughly 3.9× of the time gap before any hardware difference.
headline_items: Paper SOD 0.6B is 120 steps at 1,052.3 s/step; issue reports 1,042 s/step, only 1% apart. The released script defaults to about 469 steps, explaining roughly 3.9× of the time gap before any hardware difference.

Measured: actual `_apply_token_kl_regularizer` took 7.81 s median for 1,024 synthetic trajectories × 128 tokens, including the shipped detailed log writer; this short sequence is not a full-training estimate.

Source gap: `run_sod.sh` sets one epoch and batch 64 but no explicit stop step. The trainer supports `trainer.total_training_steps`; the paper says 120 (0.6B) and 150 (1.7B). The loop has no convergence-based stop criterion.
